question: Does learning capacity provide a theoretically justified, reproducible, and practically useful measure of effective model dimensionality across neural and nonparametric models, and does it independently explain generalization and double descent better than prior effective-dimension measures?

key_findings.claim: The paper's most defensible contribution is a broad empirical operationalization of finite-sample learning capacity across parametric and nonparametric models, not the thermodynamic definition itself.
key_findings.evidence: The paper starts from LaMont and Wiggins' partition-function learning capacity, then proposes estimating an average predictive cross-entropy over many training-set sizes and differentiating its fitted learning curve. It applies the procedure to fully connected networks, LeNet, AllCNN, WideResNet, RNNs, LSTMs, random forests, and k-nearest neighbors. This breadth and the attempt to put all models on one sample-size axis are useful, but the thermodynamic analogy and heat-capacity definition predate the paper.

key_findings.claim: The implemented estimator is not shown to estimate the Bayesian partition-function quantity that the theory defines.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 1-4 define Z(N), U(N), and C(N) by integrating a prior-weighted Gibbs posterior over parameters. Equation 9 instead averages held-out log loss from independently optimized point predictors across bootstrap samples, folds, and random initializations. Those SGD solutions are neither posterior draws nor a Bayesian predictive mixture, and no theorem proves that the cross-validated learning-curve derivative converges to the partition-function derivative. Appendix G concedes that exact capacity is optimizer independent while the numerical estimate can depend on the optimizer.

key_findings.claim: As a model-selection signal, learning capacity is computationally circular and has not been shown to improve decisions prospectively.
key_findings.evidence: To estimate C at one target sample size, the method directly measures held-out predictive log loss at roughly fourteen or fifteen sample sizes, using four bootstrap datasets, five folds, and five random initializations: about one hundred trained models per N. It then differentiates the fitted held-out-loss curve. The paper reports roughly 35,000 neural-network trainings plus about 10,000 random-forest or k-nearest-neighbor fits. Because held-out loss is already the selection target, the paper does not establish that its derivative yields a cheaper or better architecture decision than ordinary cross-validation under matched compute.

key_findings.claim: The reported freezing and saturation behavior is partly imposed by the curve-fitting family rather than independently discovered from the data.
key_findings.evidence: A preliminary polynomial fit explicitly constrains U to decrease and C to increase. The main fit assumes a sigmoid C(N)=a/[1+exp(-c log N+b)] and integrates it analytically to U, so monotonic growth and finite lower and upper plateaus are built into the estimator. Several observed curves, including AllCNN, LSTM, and unconstrained tree or neighbor models, do not reach a clear upper plateau in the measured range. The results support descriptive sigmoid-like fits for selected cases, not a model-free discovery that all learners freeze at both extremes.

key_findings.claim: The cross-architecture evidence for selecting lower-capacity models is weak and task dependent.
key_findings.evidence: Within each architecture, increasing N generally raises fitted capacity while lowering held-out loss, producing the strongly negative correlations reported in Figure 2. Across architectures at fixed N, however, Table 1 reports average Kendall correlations of only 0.40 on MNIST, 0.22 on CIFAR-10, and -0.03 on WikiText-2 for the desired association between capacity and loss. Only two architecture families are compared per modality, so the claim that capacity correlates well with test loss in almost all cases exceeds the evidence.

key_findings.claim: Capacity estimates are often too uncertain to support crisp architecture rankings.
key_findings.evidence: Representative reported estimates include 609 plus or minus 560 for the fully connected MNIST model and 231 plus or minus 204 for LeNet; on CIFAR-10 the reported AllCNN and WideResNet estimates are 4,571 plus or minus 1,700 and 5,805 plus or minus 1,145. The intervals overlap heavily, and the paper does not propagate all resampling, training, curve-family, or derivative uncertainty into a prospective probability that one architecture is better.

key_findings.claim: The double-descent result is a narrow reparameterization of measured learning curves and does not establish priority over earlier effective-dimensionality explanations.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 studies one-hidden-layer MNIST networks with widths 10-100 and width-scaled ResNet-18 models on CIFAR-10 with label noise. Plotting held-out loss against the capacity derived from those same learning curves largely removes the nonmonotonic width trend, although one high-N fit is nonsignificant. Maddox, Benton, and Wilson had already connected Hessian effective dimensionality to posterior contraction, model selection, test loss, and double descent in 2020. The target's distinctive element is differentiation over sample size and a nonparametric extension, not the first effective-dimension account of double descent.

key_findings.claim: The PAC-Bayes comparison is mixed and does not validate a general equivalence between learning capacity and generalization complexity.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 reports a Kendall correlation of 0.99 with p=4e-9 for fully connected MNIST networks but only 0.20 with p=0.37 for LeNet. The PAC-Bayes quantity uses an approximate block-diagonal Kronecker-factored Hessian and is tested on only these two MNIST architecture families. Numerical similarity in one family supports a local sanity check, not broad interchangeability across modern models, nonparametric learners, or losses.

key_findings.claim: The PAC-Bayes derivation conflates population and empirical error and relies on a deliberately loose bound.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 11 is introduced as a looser form of a PAC-Bayes bound with the usual square-root dependence removed. The surrounding text then substitutes e(Q)=integral Q(w) H-hat(w) dw even though H-hat was defined as empirical negative log likelihood, so that expression is empirical risk rather than population error. The Gibbs variational identity can motivate a free-energy analogy, but the displayed steps do not prove that the generalization coefficient is the empirical learning-capacity estimator.

key_findings.claim: The main-text Gaussian formula is presented outside the regime in which the appendix derives it.
key_findings.evidence: For a quadratic Gaussian model, Appendix F gives the exact capacity C(N)=one half times the sum over i of [N lambda_i/(N lambda_i+epsilon)] squared. Equation 5 in the main text instead summarizes C as p/2 minus an epsilon-weighted inverse-Hessian term without displaying N. Appendix F obtains that expansion only when lambda_i is much larger than epsilon/N and then invokes p approximately equal to N. Those conditions conflict with the paper's central overparameterized p much larger than N motivation, so the approximation cannot be read as a general deep-network identity.

key_findings.claim: Appendix C contains two explicit singular-learning-theory errors that invalidate its illustrative calculations as printed.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 21 prints C(N)=-N^(-2) partial_N U=K, contradicting the paper's own definition C=-N^2 partial_N U; for U=K/N the printed expression would be K/N^4. The following Remark 1 sets a constant loss H(w)=1 in the sublevel-volume definition and then claims shell scaling K=p. For epsilon approaching zero that sublevel set is empty, its volume is zero, and log volume is undefined; a regular quadratic loss would instead produce the familiar p/2 coefficient.

key_findings.claim: The asymptotic free-energy expansion in Appendix C silently omits the leading risk or entropy term.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 18 writes the expected free energy as K log N plus lower-order terms. In general singular learning theory includes a leading term proportional to N times the optimal population loss or entropy unless the loss has been explicitly centered or the realizable optimum is zero. Neither restriction is stated there. Consequently constant capacity implies U(N)=U-infinity+K/N, not that the raw predictive test loss itself must scale as 1/N on noisy classification or language data.

key_findings.claim: The MCMC appendix replaces predictive negative log likelihood by probability error without a valid equality.
key_findings.evidence: The posterior predictive log loss for one new datum is -log[Z(N+1)/Z(N)]=-log E_posterior[p_w(y|x)]. Equation 16 instead uses 1-Z(N+1)/Z(N), which equals posterior mean probability error and matches -log r only as an unstated first-order approximation near r=1. The subsequent changing-N chain is coarser still. This mismatch makes the much larger and noisier MCMC capacity estimates a change of estimand rather than a clean validation of Equation 9.

key_findings.claim: The Gaussian integration appendix contains a local sign contradiction.
key_findings.evidence: After completing the square, Equation 36 prints the epsilon-squared b_i term in -log Z divided by N with a positive sign, although Gaussian integration gives a negative contribution. Equation 37 immediately uses the negative sign. The later result is consistent with the algebra, but the adjacent formulas cannot both be correct as printed.

key_findings.claim: Extending one sample-size learning-curve statistic to random forests and k-nearest neighbors is useful, but it weakens the claim that the statistic measures parameter-space dimensionality.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 shows qualitatively sensible changes when tree leaf counts or neighbor counts restrict flexibility, and Appendix E expands the random-forest sweep. Yet these estimators have no common smooth parameter posterior, Hessian, or fixed p matching the thermodynamic derivation. The results support learning capacity as a descriptive slope or curvature of held-out performance versus N; they do not establish a shared microscopic dimension across neural networks, trees, and neighbor rules.

key_findings.claim: The paper is not reproducible enough to support its compute-intensive numerical claims.
key_findings.evidence: All 28 pages, ten figures, and the single table were rendered and inspected. The paper reports tens of thousands of model fits and gives broad architecture and optimizer details, but it provides no first-party repository, source archive, executable command, environment lock, raw learning curves, seed manifest, trained checkpoint, or machine-readable result table. Exact-title, identifier, OpenReview, author-page, and repository searches found no released artifact linked to this work.

method.core_idea: Treat the number of training examples N as inverse temperature, define a model's learning capacity as the second derivative of its log partition function with respect to N, and estimate that quantity from the slope of a fitted cross-validated predictive learning curve.
method.mechanism: The theoretical construction forms Z(N)=integral phi(w) exp[-N H-hat(w)] dw, defines average energy U=-partial_N log Z, and learning capacity C=-N^2 partial_N U=N^2 partial_N^2 log Z. The implementation samples training subsets of different sizes, runs bootstrap k-fold training with multiple random initializations, averages held-out cross-entropy to estimate U(N), fits a monotone sigmoid capacity as a function of log N through an analytically integrated U curve, and compares the resulting C across architectures, widths, datasets, and classical estimators.
assumptions: Training-set size N can be treated as an inverse temperature while the data distribution and model family remain fixed.
The prior-weighted Gibbs partition function meaningfully represents the trained learner being studied.
Cross-validated point-estimate predictive loss can stand in for the posterior average energy even though the optimizer does not sample the Gibbs posterior.
Bootstrap samples, folds, and random initializations adequately capture estimator variation.
Learning capacity is monotone in N and is well approximated by a sigmoid in log N with finite plateaus.
Held-out cross-entropy curves are smooth enough that their derivatives are scientifically stable under the chosen fit.
Different architecture families are comparable at the same N despite unmatched parameters, optimization, and compute.
The Gaussian Hessian approximation is informative when eigenvalues dominate prior precision divided by N.
Approximate Kronecker-factored Hessians retain the relevant PAC-Bayes complexity ordering.
The same learning-curve derivative has a coherent effective-dimension interpretation for neural networks, random forests, and k-nearest neighbors.
The observed N and width ranges are broad enough to reveal freezing, saturation, and double-descent structure rather than fit-boundary effects.

techniques.role: Maps sample size to inverse temperature and predictive loss to average energy.
Defines the theoretical capacity through derivatives of a prior-weighted Gibbs evidence integral.
Estimates predictive average energy on held-out folds over many training-set sizes.
Repeats subset construction to estimate variability in the learning curve.
Regularizes an otherwise unstable numerical derivative by fitting a monotone saturating capacity curve in log sample size.
Connects a quadratic Gaussian approximation to parameter-space effective dimension.
Compares fitted capacity with a posterior-complexity quantity based on approximate curvature.
Replots width-dependent predictive loss against fitted capacity to seek a monotone coordinate.
Provides an alternative posterior-inspired estimator in Appendix B, albeit with a changed loss expression.
Relates asymptotic constant capacity to singular-learning-theory complexity.

evaluations.setting: Fully connected networks and LeNet on MNIST, AllCNN and WideResNet on CIFAR-10, and RNN and LSTM models on WikiText-2
evaluations.metric: fitted learning capacity, held-out cross-entropy, and Kendall rank correlation
evaluations.result: Capacity generally rises with N within an architecture while predictive loss falls, but cross-architecture capacity-loss correlations average only 0.40, 0.22, and -0.03 on the three modalities and several uncertainty intervals overlap strongly.
evaluations.baseline: Raw parameter count and direct held-out predictive loss for two architecture families per modality.

evaluations.setting: Fully connected and LeNet MNIST models
evaluations.metric: rank correlation between learning capacity and an approximate PAC-Bayes complexity
evaluations.result: The reported Kendall correlation is 0.99 with p=4e-9 for the fully connected family but 0.20 with p=0.37 for LeNet, so the agreement is architecture dependent.
evaluations.baseline: A block-diagonal Kronecker-factored Hessian PAC-Bayes calculation over approximately 2,800 models.

evaluations.setting: Width sweeps for one-hidden-layer MNIST classifiers and width-scaled ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 classifiers with label noise
evaluations.metric: held-out loss versus parameter count and versus fitted learning capacity
evaluations.result: The familiar nonmonotonic width trend becomes mostly increasing when plotted against capacity, though one large-N regression is nonsignificant and the capacity coordinate was itself derived from held-out learning curves.
evaluations.baseline: Parameter count as the complexity coordinate; no comparison to earlier Hessian effective dimensionality under matched data and compute.

evaluations.setting: Random forests and k-nearest-neighbor classifiers on synthetic and tabular datasets
evaluations.metric: capacity curves under changes in maximum leaves or neighbor count
evaluations.result: Capacity responds qualitatively to imposed flexibility limits and often saturates when a leaf cap binds, demonstrating that the empirical learning-curve statistic can be computed without neural parameters.
evaluations.baseline: Unrestricted or differently regularized tree and neighbor estimators rather than a common Bayesian posterior model.

evaluations.setting: Cross-validation estimator versus Appendix B MCMC-style estimator
evaluations.metric: estimated average energy and capacity curves
evaluations.result: The MCMC route yields much larger and noisier capacities and a poorer average-energy match. Because Equation 16 substitutes probability error for negative log predictive probability, the comparison does not cleanly validate one estimator against the same target quantity.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's bootstrap cross-validation and sigmoid-fit estimator.

evaluations.setting: Paper-level source, visual, mathematical, and artifact audit
evaluations.metric: page coverage, figures, tables, equation consistency, and reproducibility assets
evaluations.result: All 28 pages, ten figures, one table, appendices A-G, and displayed derivations were inspected. The audit found unproven theory-to-estimator equivalence, fit-imposed saturation, several explicit appendix equation errors, and no first-party code, raw results, environment, checkpoints, or rerun commands.
evaluations.baseline: The level of evidence required to reproduce the reported roughly 45,000 model fits and distinguish estimator behavior from curve-fitting assumptions.

limitations: No consistency theorem connects the cross-validated point-predictor learning curve to the prior-weighted Bayesian partition function.
Estimating capacity requires direct held-out-loss measurements and about one hundred fits per sample size, making it costly and circular as a selection proxy.
Monotonicity and saturation are built into the main sigmoid fit and partly into the preliminary polynomial fit.
Only two neural architecture families are compared for each input modality.
Cross-architecture Kendall correlations are small or absent, and uncertainty intervals overlap substantially.
The double-descent experiments cover narrow MNIST and CIFAR-10 width sweeps and do not test modern large-scale transfer.
The PAC-Bayes comparison is positive for one family and statistically unsupported for LeNet.
The Gaussian approximation invoked in the main text assumes a spectral and p approximately N regime that need not hold for p much larger than N networks.
The singular-learning appendix omits an asymptotic leading-risk term and contains a wrong N-power and an invalid constant-loss example.
The MCMC appendix substitutes one minus predictive probability for negative log predictive probability without declaring an approximation.
The empirical quantity depends on optimizer, early stopping, regularization, and fit family even though the theoretical quantity is claimed to be optimizer independent.
Random forests and nearest-neighbor models lack the smooth shared parameter-posterior geometry used by the motivating derivation.
No independent prospective model-selection experiment asks whether capacity chooses a better learner than direct validation loss under matched compute.
No first-party code, raw learning curves, seeds, environment, or machine-readable results are released.
Citation indexes contain later applications and methodological successors but no identified independent full replication of the estimator across the claimed model breadth.
failure_modes: A fitted sigmoid can manufacture apparent freezing or saturation when the observed learning curve has not reached either regime.
Small noise in held-out loss can become large error after differentiation, even when the original fit appears visually smooth.
Comparing capacities across architectures can reverse or disappear when training compute, optimizer, augmentation, or regularization changes.
The selection procedure can spend far more compute reconstructing a derivative than direct cross-validation would need to choose a model.
An SGD point estimate can be mistaken for a Gibbs-posterior sample, creating unjustified thermodynamic interpretations.
Irreducible predictive entropy can be dropped, leading a constant-capacity asymptotic to be misread as raw test loss proportional to 1/N.
A wide, overlapping confidence interval can be collapsed into a deterministic architecture ranking.
The same capacity value can hide different learning-curve shapes, data regimes, or failure mechanisms.
A fit that works on small vision and language benchmarks can fail at larger scale where optimizer, data mixture, and emergence change with N.
Tree leaf caps or neighbor hyperparameters can create artificial plateaus that look like intrinsic model dimensionality.
Incorrect appendix equations can propagate into downstream RLCT or MCMC implementations without executable tests.
Replotting a target metric against a derivative of that target can remove double descent without yielding a causal or independently measurable explanation.
reusable_insights: A model-complexity measure should distinguish its exact mathematical object from the numerical proxy actually computed.
Learning-curve derivatives are a useful common descriptive language across model classes when they are not overinterpreted as literal parameter dimension.
Derivative estimators should report sensitivity across splines, Gaussian processes, monotone fits, and unconstrained local methods rather than one saturating family.
Prospective model-selection tests should compare decision quality and total compute against direct cross-validation, parameter count, Hessian effective dimension, and local learning coefficients.
Within-architecture and across-architecture correlations answer different questions and should never be pooled rhetorically.
A capacity estimate should propagate subset, fold, seed, optimizer, hyperparameter, and curve-fit uncertainty through to the final ranking.
Exact solvable models are valuable unit tests: every approximation should recover the Gaussian formula and correct asymptotic risk floor.
Nonparametric extensions can be framed cleanly as effective data demand or learning-curve curvature without claiming a universal posterior geometry.
Double-descent explanations are stronger when the complexity signal is measured independently of the test-loss curve it is meant to explain.
Releasing raw per-run learning curves is more important than releasing only fitted capacities because it permits alternative estimators and falsification.
open_questions: Can a theorem relate cross-validated point-predictor learning-curve derivatives to Bayesian heat capacity under explicit optimizer and posterior-concentration assumptions?
Does learning capacity select architectures prospectively better than direct validation loss under identical fit and compute budgets?
Which nonparametric derivative estimator remains calibrated when the true capacity is nonmonotone or does not saturate?
How stable are rankings across optimizers, schedules, augmentations, regularizers, seeds, and prior choices?
Can a small-model pilot predict the large-model capacity curve without assuming the very scaling law under test?
What negative controls distinguish genuine effective dimension from a plateau imposed by a leaf cap, early stopping, or fit boundary?
Do local learning coefficients, Hessian effective dimension, and learning capacity make different prospective predictions on the same modern transformer suite?
Can learning capacity be estimated from checkpoints, gradients, or held-out predictions without training hundreds of models at many sample sizes?
How should irreducible entropy and distribution shift be separated from the 1/N learnable component of predictive risk?
Does the empirical quantity remain coherent for reinforcement learning, where samples are dependent and the policy changes the data distribution?
Can a hierarchical model propagate all resampling and curve-family uncertainty into calibrated capacity intervals?
Which observed double-descent phenomena remain after comparing against Maddox-style Hessian effective dimension and current singularity-aware measures?
Can an open benchmark with raw curves, fixed compute, and preregistered selection decisions independently replicate the claimed breadth across neural, tree, and neighbor models?

competitive_landscape.title: On the correspondence between thermodynamics and inference
competitive_landscape.difference: LaMont and Wiggins establish the sample-size-as-inverse-temperature correspondence and learning-capacity concept used by the target. The reviewed paper's contribution is a new cross-validation estimator and broad deep-learning application, not the original definition.

competitive_landscape.title: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Deep Models: Effective Dimensionality Revisited
competitive_landscape.difference: Maddox, Benton, and Wilson use Hessian effective dimensionality for posterior contraction, model selection, generalization, and double descent, with released code. It predates and undermines the target's priority language about effective dimensionality resolving double descent; the target differs by differentiating over sample size and including nonparametric models.

competitive_landscape.title: Does the Data Induce Capacity Control in Deep Learning?
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang, Mao, and Chaudhari study data-dependent capacity using sloppy Hessian or Fisher spectra and PAC-Bayes effective dimension. The target replaces direct curvature with a sample-size learning-curve derivative while retaining the same broad capacity-control program.

competitive_landscape.title: Effective dimension of machine learning models
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbas et al. define a local and global effective dimension from Fisher information and derive a generalization bound before the target. Their object measures local model geometry, while learning capacity differentiates predictive performance over sample size; this further limits any claim to introducing effective dimensionality or its generalization connection.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
competitive_landscape.difference: Nakkiran et al. formalize effective model complexity and empirical double descent across model size, data, and training time. The target proposes learning capacity as one alternate horizontal axis but evaluates a much narrower subset of the phenomenon.

competitive_landscape.title: Fantastic Generalization Measures and Where to Find Them
competitive_landscape.difference: Jiang et al. benchmark many generalization measures across controlled interventions and expose frequent failures of correlation. The target evaluates far fewer architecture families and does not subject learning capacity to an equivalent intervention matrix.

competitive_landscape.title: Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep (Stochastic) Neural Networks with Many More Parameters than Training Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Dziugaite and Roy optimize stochastic neural-network posteriors to obtain nonvacuous PAC-Bayes bounds. The target uses a looser analytic analogy and an approximate Hessian comparison rather than computing a full bound for its model suite.

competitive_landscape.title: The Training Process of Many Deep Networks Explores the Same Low-Dimensional Manifold
competitive_landscape.difference: Mao et al. measure a low-dimensional prediction manifold across deep networks using information geometry. Submitted earlier in May 2023, it offers a more direct geometric capacity notion; the target instead infers a scalar dimension from sample-size response.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimating Real Log Canonical Thresholds
competitive_landscape.difference: Imai develops numerical estimation of real log canonical thresholds, the asymptotic singular-model quantity invoked in Appendix C. It targets the mathematical singularity coefficient directly, whereas the reviewed paper estimates a finite-N predictive learning-curve derivative.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning is Singular, and That's Good
competitive_landscape.difference: Murfet et al. foreground singular models and real log canonical thresholds as the relevant asymptotic complexity for deep networks. The target's Appendix C imports that theory, but its finite-N SGD cross-validation estimator is not proven to equal the RLCT quantity.

competitive_landscape.title: The Local Learning Coefficient: A Singularity-Aware Complexity Measure
competitive_landscape.difference: Lau et al. estimate a local learning coefficient with SGLD, validate against analytically known models, and study ResNets and transformers while distinguishing higher-order singular structure hidden by Hessian rank. It explicitly positions finite-sample learning capacity near the same theory but provides a more local, singularity-aware competitor.

competitive_landscape.title: A Two-Scale Complexity Measure for Deep Learning Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This work derives a two-scale generalization complexity and a scalable layerwise approximation. It competes on practical computability and bound structure rather than requiring dozens of full retrainings over sample sizes.

competitive_landscape.title: NGD converges to less degenerate solutions than SGD
competitive_landscape.difference: This singular-learning-theory study compares the degeneracy of solutions selected by natural gradient and stochastic gradient descent using local learning coefficients. It directly illustrates why the target's optimizer-dependent numerical proxy cannot inherit optimizer independence without qualification.

competitive_landscape.title: Modes of Sequence Models and Learning Coefficients
competitive_landscape.difference: This work connects learning coefficients to modes, thresholds, and resolution in sequence models. It develops structure-specific singular complexity beyond the target's single scalar capacity curve for RNN and LSTM language models.

competitive_landscape.title: An Effective Gram Matrix Characterizes Generalization in Deep Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Chaudhari derive a differential-equation and effective-Gram-matrix characterization of the generalization gap and test predictive structure in modern image networks. It is a more mechanistic continuation of the same team's data-dependent-capacity program than a fitted scalar learning curve.

competitive_landscape.title: An Analytical Characterization of Sloppiness in Neural Networks: Insights from Linear Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Mao et al. derive phase boundaries and low-dimensional hyper-ribbon structure in solvable models, offering an analytic account of effective geometry. It cites the learning-capacity line but does not independently reproduce the target's cross-validation estimator.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Uncertainty in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: This direct-citing work measures predictive uncertainty across data and model scales in modern vision and language settings and notes that simple 1/N behavior need not hold in overparameterized regimes. It is adjacent scaling evidence, not an independent validation of learning capacity.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Utility of Virtual Staining for Downstream Applications as it relates to Task Network Capacity
competitive_landscape.difference: This biomedical application cites network capacity while studying virtual staining and downstream tasks. It demonstrates conceptual reuse in a new domain but does not replicate or falsify the target's estimator under its original benchmark protocol.

competitive_landscape.title: The Normalized Maximum Likelihood for Regular Non-Smooth Models: Measure-Theoretic Foundations and Geometric Sampling
competitive_landscape.difference: This direct-citing work develops exact normalized-maximum-likelihood foundations and geometric sampling for non-smooth models. It offers an information-criterion route that does not estimate complexity by differentiating a cross-validated learning curve and is not a replication of the target.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that learning capacity is a universal, data-dependent effective dimensionality that can be estimated for both parametric and nonparametric models, predicts model performance, connects to PAC-Bayes and singular learning theory, and removes double descent when used instead of parameter count.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The authors run a large cross-validation study across image, language, synthetic, and tabular tasks; fit sample-size capacity curves; compare two neural families per modality; relate one MNIST family strongly to an approximate PAC-Bayes quantity; replot two width sweeps; and extend the empirical calculation to trees and nearest neighbors.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The genuinely distinctive contribution is a broad finite-N empirical learning-curve derivative presented in a thermodynamic language and applied to both neural and nonparametric models. The learning-capacity definition comes from LaMont and Wiggins; Hessian effective dimensionality had already been used for model selection and double descent by Maddox et al.; and the same team had already pursued data-induced capacity through sloppy curvature. The paper does not prove that its cross-validated point-estimate proxy estimates the defined Bayesian quantity, and the main sigmoid fit imposes monotonic saturation. Its model-selection evidence is circular and weak across architectures, with large overlapping uncertainties, while several appendix equations are incorrect as printed. Current local-learning-coefficient, two-scale, effective-Gram, and sloppiness work provides more direct or singularity-aware alternatives. Citation searches through 2026-08-23 found later applications and methodological successors but no independent full replication of the reported estimator breadth. Credit this as an ambitious descriptive unification and hypothesis generator, not a validated universal dimension or first effective-dimension explanation of double descent.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete hashed 28-page arXiv v2 source updated 2024-10-20, including all references and Appendices A-G. Rendered and visually inspected every page, Figure 1, Figures 2-5, Figures S1-S4, and Table 1; checked the displayed derivations on pages 19, 20, 24, and 25 at page-level resolution. The audit distinguishes the exact Gibbs partition-function definition from the bootstrap five-fold, five-initialization point-predictor estimator; checks the constrained polynomial and sigmoid assumptions; separates within-architecture from across-architecture correlations; and traces the Gaussian, PAC-Bayes, MCMC, and singular-learning calculations. It identifies the wrong N-power and invalid constant-loss example in Appendix C, the log-to-linear predictive-loss substitution in Appendix B, the restricted Gaussian approximation, and the sign contradiction in Appendix F. Exact-title, arXiv-identifier, OpenReview, author-page, GitHub, and artifact searches found no first-party code or data release; the ICLR 2024 OpenReview entry is a changed-title submission, remains marked submitted rather than accepted, and exposes no code URL. Primary-source competitor and citation-chain checks were carried through 2026-08-23, distinguishing foundational sources, the unacknowledged Maddox effective-dimension priority conflict, same-team predecessors and successors, direct later citations, and singularity-aware alternatives. The few later applications are not independent replications. No shared projection, aggregate, or generated web data was modified.
